title: Rabi' al-Awwal: love of the Prophet ﷺ
hookLine: a month to study his life, celebrated or not
tomorrow: a gift brought down from the highest night. what was it?

lines: A PARTY, OR A PHONE CALL.
cards: Some families throw a birthday party with a cake and a playlist; some barely mention the date and just call. Both can love the person.

Rabi' al-Awwal is the month tradition gives for the birth of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and Muslims mark it in different ways. Amira's auntie is hosting a mawlid, an evening of poems and stories about his life.
Her dad, Yusuf, isn't going. So who's right?

teach.h: IF YE LOVE ALLAH, FOLLOW ME.
teach.b: Start with what both of them would say. The Qur'an, in Pickthall's words: "If ye love Allah, follow me; Allah will love you and forgive you your sins." Love, in that verse, isn't only a feeling; it shows up as following.

And a report in Sahih al-Bukhari says none of you truly believes until the Prophet is dearer to him than his father, his children and all people. So nobody in this family is arguing about whether to love him.
They're arguing about how to show it.

Those who hold a mawlid say that gathering to recite poems in his praise, tell his life and send blessings on him is a good way to stir that love; and he himself marked the day he was born, by fasting on Mondays.
Those who don't say the companions held no yearly birthday gathering, so the surer way is to keep his sunna every day of the year.

Here's what both sides share, worth telling a friend: the month is a reason to read his life, the seerah. A celebration that never opens it misses the point, and so does a refusal that never opens it either.
That's love him by following: wherever you land on the party, open the story.

how: In Rabi' al-Awwal some Muslims hold mawlid gatherings with poems, stories and salawat, while others keep no special observance. Families on both sides may use the month to read the Prophet's life (seerah) together.

o: the month the Qur'an was fully written down
the month tradition gives for the Prophet's birth
the month of fasting before the pilgrimage

games.q: the month and the love — tap the pairs.
p: if ye love Allah, follow me
the fast on the day he was born

s: Muslims who skip the mawlid don't love the Prophet
they show love by keeping his sunna; the debate is about how, not whether.
in 3:31, love for God is tied to following the Prophet
if ye love Allah, follow me; Allah will love you.
every Muslim marks Rabi' al-Awwal the same way
some hold poems, stories and blessings; others keep the month for quiet study.

games.q: your kid asks: if we don't have a party for the Prophet, does that mean we don't love him? what could you say at dinner?
o: love shows up as following him; people differ on parties.
yes. families who really love him always throw one.
love is private, so what you do doesn't matter.
games.why: 'If ye love Allah, follow me': the Qur'an ties love to following. Muslims differ on the mawlid, not on loving him.

practice: Say the verse out loud, slowly, in any translation: if you love God, follow me. Then read one short passage of his life, the seerah, from a book you trust, out loud if you can, for as long as the sit runs.
One page is enough to begin.

carryVoice: The line for today: love him by following, and open the story, party or no party. Five of fourteen, done.
